<text:style bold="true">Handles</text:style>

With the Select tool a click on a vector object selects it and shows the handles that
resize, skew and turn it (see Rotation below). A<text:style bold="true"> double click on one of those handles</text:style>
shows instead the handles of its points, described here: small marks that are dragged
with the mouse to change the object itself, not only its position. A double click on
one of them goes back to resizing and turning. The object is moved by dragging its
body (or its outline); the handles of the points change its shape. Selecting another
object starts again with the handles that resize and turn.
A line (the Line object, selected alone) is the exception: a click shows at once the handles of its two
ends, and it has no handles to resize, skew or turn it.

<text:style bold="true">Square handles</text:style> are points of the object: the ends of a line, the corners of a
rectangle, the vertices of a polygon or a polyline, the points of a curve or of a
path. Dragging one moves that point only. The constraints of the drawing are kept
while you drag (the other points that are tied to it follow), the snap helpers work,
and a point that is Fixed does not move: the status bar says "Part of the selection
is fixed".

<text:style bold="true">Round handles</text:style> are parameters of the object, not points:

- Rectangle: a round handle on the top side, a little to the right of the top left
  corner. Dragging it to the right makes the corners rounder (the radius cannot be
  more than half of the shorter side). It is the same as the Corner radius property.
- Ellipse and circle: the centre (square handle, it moves the whole ellipse), a
  round handle on the right (horizontal radius) and one below the centre (vertical
  radius). For a circle (Circle, equal radii, checked in the properties) there is
  only the first one and the radius is the same on both axes.
- Arc: the same three handles of the ellipse, plus two round handles at the two ends
  of the arc: dragging them changes the start angle and the end angle.
- Arc made by Fillet: one round handle in the middle of the arc. It changes the
  radius of the fillet, and the lines that make the corner follow (the rest of the
  corner stays where it is).
- Curve and path: the points of the curve are square handles; the control points of
  a Bezier path are small circles, joined with a dotted line to their point. A Shift
  click adds or takes out a point from the selected points: dragging one of them
  moves all of them together. A right click on a point offers to remove it (see
  Right Click).

<text:style bold="true">Rasters show the resize / turn box at once</text:style>: a click on a picture selects it and shows the
handles that resize, turn and deform it (a drag inside the box moves the picture). Click outside the box
to deselect it. The arrow keys of the keyboard also move a selected picture.

There are no handles for a fill made with the Paint bucket (it follows the lines
that close it), for the objects of a locked or hidden layer. The corner and the
edges of the page are handles too: dragging them changes the size of the page.

<text:style bold="true">Groups, and many objects: the box with eight handles</text:style>

When the selection is a<text:style bold="true"> group</text:style> (Ctrl+G joins the selected objects in a group,
Ctrl+Shift+G splits it again) the objects do not show their own handles: the group
has a dashed box with<text:style bold="true"> eight square handles</text:style>, four on the corners and four on the
middle of the sides. Dragging a handle stretches the whole group: the side (or
corner) opposite to the handle stays where it is. A corner handle stretches in both
directions; with Shift pressed it keeps the proportions. A side handle stretches in
one direction only. A group cannot be reduced to less than 2% of its size. A group
that has been turned is stretched along its own sides, not along the sides of the
page.

<image:base64 col="0" width="76" wrap="none"></image:base64>

<text:style bold="true">Rotation</text:style>

<text:style bold="true">A selected vector object shows at once the handles that deform and turn it</text:style> (for a group
too): the box of the selection is shown in orange, with a small cross at its centre
(the centre of the rotation), eight handles and one more round handle outside the box,
above the middle of the top side (on another side if that place is not on the screen).
To edit the points of the object, double click on one of these handles.

- The four<text:style bold="true"> square handles on the corners</text:style> stretch the selection: the opposite corner
  stays where it is. Keep Shift pressed to keep the proportions.
- The four<text:style bold="true"> diamond handles in the middle of the sides</text:style> skew the selection: the side
  opposite to the handle stays where it is and the dragged side slides along its own
  direction (the status bar shows the angle of the skew). A rectangle becomes a
  polygon and an ellipse becomes a path when they are skewed; texts and arcs cannot
  be skewed and are left as they are. A picture (raster) can be skewed: it is
  resampled into a new, larger picture that holds the sheared one. As long as the
  picture stays selected with its second-mode handles the program remembers the
  original: every new skew is made from it, so nothing is lost by skewing again, and
  bringing the skew back to zero (it snaps to zero near the centre) gives back the
  original size and pixels.
- The<text:style bold="true"> round handle outside the box</text:style> turns the selection about the cross. The status
  bar shows the total angle. Counter-clockwise angles are positive. Keep Shift
  pressed to turn in steps of 15 degrees.
- If the selection has been turned, it is stretched and skewed along its own sides,
  not along the sides of the page.
- To edit the points double click on a handle; double click on a handle of a point to
  come back. A click on another object, or on an empty place, selects it and starts
  again with the handles that resize and turn. Dragging from any point
  inside the box moves the selection. A simple click (without moving) on another object
  that lies inside the box picks that object.
- It works on a group, on one object, and also on several objects selected together
  (they are deformed as a whole; reference objects are left out). Everything is one
  step of the history.

<image:base64 col="0" width="47" wrap="none"></image:base64>

The three pictures: the handles of a rectangle (four corners and the round handle of
the corner radius), the rotation mode after the double click, and the rectangle
after it was turned.

<text:style bold="true">The Rotation property.</text:style> When the selection is a group, or one rectangle, ellipse,
arc, text, path or picture, the Properties panel has the row Rotation: the angle in
degrees (from -360 to 360, counter-clockwise). Typing a value turns the object about
the centre of its box; it is applied a moment after the last key. It is also the way
to turn an object back to exactly 0 degrees. For lines, polylines and polygons there
is no such row: they are turned by moving their points, so there is nothing to type
(use the handles, or the Rotate button of the Actions panel).

<text:style bold="true">What turning does to an object:</text:style>

- Lines, arrows, polylines, polygons and curves: their points are moved to the
  turned positions.
- Rectangles, ellipses, arcs, texts, paths and pictures: the object keeps the turn
  as a property (Rotation) and its handles are drawn where the turned object has
  them, so a turned rectangle can still be resized from its corners. A turned
  picture cannot be cropped or corrected in perspective: turn it back to 0 first.
- Copies made by Offset, Mirror or Array, and the arcs of a Fillet, follow their
  original and are not turned by themselves: turn the original.
- Everything is one step of the history: Ctrl+Z undoes the whole rotation.
